slots.X: Two reports concern ozone: near-city downwind ozone increases on a sunny day, while satellite observations indicate a thinner protective stratospheric ozone layer. Build separate causal models for (A) local NOₓ/VOC sunlight-driven surface ozone and (B) long-lived CFC compounds releasing reactive chlorine under stratospheric UV that can destroy ozone catalytically. Explain why a local surface ozone reading cannot determine stratospheric ozone depletion and propose a distinct measurement for each.
slots.Y: The protective stratospheric ozone layer is continuously formed and destroyed through sunlight-driven atmospheric chemistry. Its depletion means a reduction in stratospheric O₃ abundance, allowing more harmful UV-B to reach the surface; this is distinct from excess ground-level ozone pollution. Certain long-lived ozone-depleting chemicals, notably chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) once used in some refrigeration and aerosol applications, can survive long enough to reach the stratosphere. Strong ultraviolet light breaks some CFC molecules and releases reactive chlorine atoms, which participate in repeated ozone-destroying reactions. Other ozone-depleting substances and atmospheric conditions also matter: do not infer a unique global ozone trend from one local pollution reading.
slots.Z: For ground-level ozone, NOₓ and volatile organic compounds can undergo sunlight-driven photochemistry and downwind transport that enhances O₃ near the surface under suitable conditions. For stratospheric depletion, some long-lived CFCs reach upper air, undergo UV photolysis, and release reactive Cl·. A simplified catalytic cycle Cl·+O₃→ClO·+O₂, ClO·+O→Cl·+O₂ regenerates chlorine, net O₃+O→2O₂. The model is bounded: real ozone chemistry depends on additional atmospheric conditions. Satellite/ozonesonde vertical stratospheric measurements address protective ozone; ground-level calibrated sensors address local pollution. One does not establish the other.
slots.W: Construct and discriminate two altitude-dependent ozone chemical models, identify the catalytic species and choose independent evidence for each.

subtopics.title: Applied sustainable chemical decisions

slots.X: A school compares three used packages: untreated paper placed in warm, moist managed compost, a polyethylene (PE) wrapper discarded outdoors, and a glass bottle collected for recycling. Classify each as biodegradable or ordinarily non-biodegradable under the stated conditions, distinguish microbial conversion from physical fragmentation and recyclability, then explain why these labels alone cannot decide which package has the lowest full-life-cycle impact.
slots.Y: Biodegradable and non-biodegradable describe different responses to biological decomposition, not whether an item can be recycled or whether it always has low impact. Under suitable environmental conditions, microbes and their enzymes can break many food scraps, untreated paper and plant-derived material into simpler substances; rate and final products depend on oxygen, moisture, temperature and material composition. Conventional polyethylene packaging and glass are generally non-biodegradable on ordinary environmental timescales: they are not readily mineralised by natural microbial action. Glass can be recyclable without being biodegradable. A plastic fragment becoming smaller, or a material weathering in sunlight, is not proof that microorganisms have completely broken it down.
slots.Z: Untreated paper is usually biodegradable under suitable warm moist microbial compost conditions, although decomposition can be much slower in dry or anaerobic disposal. Conventional polyethylene is generally non-biodegradable on ordinary environmental timescales; fragmenting into microplastics is not complete microbial mineralisation. Glass is non-biodegradable but may be reused or recycled, depending on collection and processing. Biodegradability, recyclability and total environmental impact are distinct. Production, transport, use, treatment and fate determine the lifecycle comparison; the stated labels alone do not establish a universal winner.
slots.W: Build the biodegradable/non-biodegradable classification using disposal conditions and distinguish it from reuse/recycling and lifecycle impact.

qrt_instances.student_task: A school compares three used packages: untreated paper placed in warm, moist managed compost, a polyethylene (PE) wrapper discarded outdoors, and a glass bottle collected for recycling. Classify each as biodegradable or ordinarily non-biodegradable under the stated conditions, distinguish microbial conversion from physical fragmentation and recyclability, then explain why these labels alone cannot decide which package has the lowest full-life-cycle impact.
qrt_instances.wrong_idea: Wrong path: a recyclable glass bottle must be biodegradable, or a polyethylene wrapper becoming smaller means it has biologically decomposed.
qrt_instances.replacement_rule: Check microbial conversion and products, identify applicable timescale and conditions, and independently model reuse/recycling as a different process from decomposition.

qrt_instances.independent_check: If untreated paper moves from wet, aerated compost to a cold, dry landfill, does it automatically become chemically non-biodegradable? Compare expected rate with a conventional PE wrapper.
